title: Horoscopes: Written in the Stars?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore astrology from a skeptical but curious angle, covering its history from ancient Babylon and other cultures, the Western and Chinese zodiac systems, sun sign and natal astrology, elemental and cardinal/fixed/mutable classifications, how charts are built, studies finding no link to compatibility or divorce, precession shifting the constellations so modern birth-date signs differ (the NASA-publicized shift), and the Reagan White House astrologer Joan Quigley. The episode also includes a sponsor read, a listener mail about Star Wars action figure name mix-ups, and sign-off.
topics: St. John's Anglican Church mural Lunenburg

segments.title: Sponsor read and Sketch Fest promo
segments.summary: Squarespace and Google sponsor read, followed by a promo for a Sketch Fest live show in Oakland.

segments.title: Opening banter and hosts' beliefs
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode as a conversation about horoscopes and astrology. Chuck says he is skeptical; Josh says he finds the subject interesting from a skeptical standpoint. They discuss past chart readings and why self-reflection can make them valuable.

segments.title: Astrology defined and ancient origins
segments.summary: Astrology is defined as the belief that distant celestial objects influence life on Earth. Early astrological systems date back about five thousand years, with Western astrology developing with the Babylonians around three thousand years ago. Astronomy and astrology were once the same discipline.

segments.title: Astrology across cultures
segments.summary: Hosts note that nearly every culture had some astrological system. They mention Aztec, Inca and Mayan zodiacs with twenty symbols, and a Chinese system with twenty-four divisions and twelve animal branches, including elemental animal subdivisions.

segments.title: Babylonian zodiac and critiques
segments.summary: Hosts describe how the Babylonians associated planets with traits, such as Mars with war, and divided the zodiac into twelve equal parts while leaving out a thirteenth constellation, Ophiuchus. They point out that the constellations do not match equal thirty-day divisions.

segments.title: Break and caveats
segments.summary: Hosts pause the discussion, joke about horoscopes, and note that astrology has many contradictory layers, so they will stick to the basics.

segments.title: Sun sign astrology and the zodiac wheel
segments.summary: Sun sign astrology is explained as the constellation behind the Sun at a person's birth. The zodiac is pictured as a circle divided into slices, and the hosts use a pie and cake analogy. The three branches of Western astrology are described: mundane, interrogatory, and natal.

segments.title: Elements, cardinal, fixed and mutable signs
segments.summary: The signs are grouped into four elements (fire, earth, air, water) and into cardinal, fixed, and mutable qualities. Tropical and sidereal astrology are contrasted. Masculine and feminine (yin and yang) classifications are mentioned, and Chuck reads his Pisces traits.

segments.title: Building a birth chart and interpretation
segments.summary: An astrological chart adds the time of birth, houses, planets and the Moon, and the astrologer's interpretation of their positions and aspects. Hosts note that an astrologer could produce many different readings from the same chart, and that a chart takes significant calculation. Josh's beef is that there is no known mechanism explaining how stars would affect personality.

segments.title: Studies, selection bias, and precession
segments.summary: Studies find no link between astrological compatibility and divorce or relationships, and selection bias is discussed as a reason people think astrology works. The hosts explain that Earth's axial wobble (precession) has shifted the constellations, so modern birth dates fall under different signs. They list the shifted date ranges, including a NASA blog post, and Chuck and Josh discuss the Gemini and Pisces shifts.

segments.title: Nancy Reagan's White House astrologer
segments.summary: Hosts describe how Joan Quigley, an astrologer, was revealed to have advised Ronald and Nancy Reagan on scheduling, including press conferences, speeches and travel. Don Regan's memoir is cited, and Quigley's book What Does Joan Say? is mentioned. Hosts also cite a poll showing declining and rising American belief in astrology.

segments.title: St. John's mural and closing topics
segments.summary: The hosts recount the St. John's Anglican Church mural in Lunenburg, Nova Scotia, which accurately depicts the night sky of December 1, 1754, and mention closing thoughts on nature versus nurture and birth order.

segments.title: Listener mail: Star Wars action figure names
segments.summary: Listener Harrison writes about Kenner's mislabeled names for two Empire Strikes Back bounty hunter figures, which were later corrected on Hasbro packaging.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and share social media and website information.
